title: Observability for AI: trace every step, log every prompt, watch drift
story:
The difficulty specific to these systems is that failure does not raise anything. Nothing throws, nothing returns a bad status, every dependency responds, and the answer is wrong. Your usual dashboard is a board of green lights describing a product that is misleading people, and no amount of refining error rates will make it turn red, because there is no error.

So the first requirement is that every step of a request is recorded — its input, its output, and an identifier that ties it to the rest of the same request. The unit of debugging here is the whole trace, because a retrieval that returned nothing, a prompt that assembled strangely and an answer that invented something are one story, and separately they are three logs that nobody can connect. Anyone who has tried to explain a bad answer from a metrics dashboard alone knows how this ends.

Record the versions of everything that can change the output, and record them on the request rather than somewhere central. The model and its version. The prompt version. Which index the retrieval hit and when it was last built. The decoding settings. Without those, reproducing anything means guessing what the state was last week, and every investigation begins by rebuilding a world that may never have existed.

Then measure the things that are not errors, because these are the only leading indicators you get. How often the system refuses. How often retrieval returns nothing, or returns something with a poor best score. The distribution of output lengths. The latency tail. The cost per request. How many answers contain a citation that failed verification. None of these is an alert on its own, and all of them are informative when they move — a refusal rate that doubles overnight means something changed, and that is true whether the change was the model, the index, a prompt edit or the users.

Since prompts contain whatever your users typed, logging them is a data decision rather than a logging decision, and it has to be made before you need the logs rather than during the incident. Redact at the boundary, set a retention period, and be able to say plainly what is kept and for how long. It is far easier to build this at the start than to retrofit it into a system that is already holding six months of everything anybody ever typed.

Record a baseline while things are working, because you cannot notice a change without one. This is the part that is obvious in hindsight and almost never done in advance: the numbers above, captured over a good week, stored somewhere durable, labelled with the versions in play. Drift and regression are both statements about a comparison, and the comparison needs a fixed point.

And keep a person reading real traces every week. A handful, sampled properly, read by someone who knows what a good answer looks like. Every team that does this finds classes of failure that no metric surfaced — the answer that is fluent and subtly beside the point, the citation that supports a different claim than the one it is attached to, the polite refusal to do something the system could easily have done. Those are invisible to aggregate measurement by construction, and they are exactly what the users will tell you about eventually anyway. Better to hear it first.

problem.name: Seeing failures that raise nothing
problem.shape: The system can be entirely wrong while every component reports success.
tell: the dashboards are green and users are reporting bad answers
a bad answer cannot be reproduced because nobody recorded which versions were in play
the logs contain the final response and not the steps that produced it
there is no record of what the numbers looked like when things were fine
problem.move: Trace every step under one request identifier with its inputs and outputs, stamp each request with the model, prompt, index and decoding versions, track the non-error indicators, capture a baseline while things work, and have a person read sampled traces every week.
problem.invariant: A wrong answer is not an error, so it can only be found by recording what the system did and comparing it with what it did before.
problem.breaks: Prompts contain user data, so recording them is a privacy decision that has to be made before the logs exist rather than during the incident that needs them.

cost.time: tracing adds work on every request and storage grows with traffic, which is the price of being able to explain anything
cost.space: full traces are large and sensitive, so retention and redaction are part of the design rather than an afterthought
cost.beats: error-rate monitoring, which stays green through the failures that matter, and end-to-end evaluation alone, which tells you something is worse without showing where

problem.practice: Take one bad answer reported by a user and try to reconstruct exactly what produced it — the retrieved passages, the assembled input, the model version, the prompt version. However far you get before you are guessing is the current state of your observability, and the first gap you hit is the first thing to build.

beats.broke: The failures that matter raise no error, so error-rate monitoring stays green while the product misleads people.
beats.fix: Trace every step under one identifier, stamp each request with the versions that shaped it, and track the non-error indicators against a baseline captured while things worked.
beats.cost: Traces are large and contain user data, so storage, redaction and retention are part of the design, and a weekly human read costs real time.

interview.q: Why do the usual monitoring signals miss the failures that matter here, and what should be recorded instead?
interview.trap: Waiting for a metric to catch a subtly wrong answer. Aggregates cannot see fluent-but-beside-the-point failures, which is why sampled human review of real traces is a requirement rather than a nicety.
interview.answer:
Because nothing fails. No exception, no bad status, every dependency answers, and the response is wrong — so the dashboard is green while the product misleads people, and refining error rates cannot help when there is no error.

What I record instead starts with the whole trace: every step's input and output under one request identifier, because an empty retrieval, a strangely assembled prompt and an invented answer are one story and three disconnected logs otherwise. Then the versions, stamped on the request — model, prompt, which index and when it was built, decoding settings — since without them reproducing a case means guessing what last week looked like.

Then the non-error indicators, which are the only leading signals available: refusal rate, empty or weak retrieval rate, output length distribution, latency tail, cost per request, and how many answers carry a citation that failed verification. None is an alert by itself; each is informative when it moves.

Because prompts contain user data, logging them is a privacy decision made before the logs exist — redaction at the boundary, a retention period, and a plain answer to what is kept.

I capture a baseline while things work, because drift and regression are comparisons and a comparison needs a fixed point. And I keep someone reading sampled traces weekly, which always surfaces failures no metric can see: the fluent answer beside the point, the citation supporting a different claim, the needless refusal.
